text: Raised cholesterol narrows arteries, including those needed for erections. Treating it can help.

title: Walnuts and erections
text: Small studies link regular nut eating, especially walnuts and pistachios, with better erectile function.

title: Watermelon and blood flow
text: Watermelon contains citrulline, which the body uses to relax blood vessels. It's a healthy treat, though not a cure.

title: Beetroot juice and circulation
text: Beetroot is rich in nitrates that help blood vessels widen. It may modestly support circulation.

title: Leafy greens for blood flow
text: Spinach, rocket and lettuce are rich in nitrates that support healthy blood vessels.

title: Swap evening alcohol for a walk together
text: A post-dinner walk instead of a second drink helps digestion, mood and intimacy.

title: Desire and thyroid medicine
text: If you take thyroid medicine and still feel low desire and tired, ask whether your dose needs checking.

title: Women's arousal also needs blood flow
text: Heart health, exercise and not smoking support women's arousal just as they do men's.

title: Vulval soreness after menopause
text: Burning or soreness of the vulva is common after menopause and treatable. Don't use harsh soaps; see a doctor if it persists.

title: Lichen sclerosus needs a doctor
text: White, itchy, fragile patches of vulval skin can be a condition called lichen sclerosus, which needs treatment.

title: Pain at the vaginal entrance
text: Pain right at the entrance can come from tight pelvic floor muscles. A women's health physiotherapist can help.

title: Pelvic floor relaxation matters too
text: Some people have muscles that are too tight, not too weak. Learning to relax them can ease pain during sex.

title: Warm-up time for women
text: Spending 20 minutes or more on touching before intercourse helps natural lubrication after menopause.

title: Orgasm and the pelvic floor
text: Stronger pelvic floor muscles are linked with stronger orgasms in both sexes.

title: Use a mirror to understand changes
text: Women who look at their vulva after menopause often feel less anxious about changes and can spot problems early.

title: Desire and hearing loss
text: Constantly saying 'pardon?' can build distance in a relationship. Hearing aids can bring couples closer.

title: Sex after cataract or eye surgery
text: Ask your eye surgeon when intimacy is safe after eye surgery — usually within a week or two.

title: After hernia repair
text: Gentle intimacy is usually fine within a couple of weeks of hernia surgery, avoiding strain. Ask your surgeon.

title: Intimacy with chronic fatigue
text: Plan intimacy for your best-energy time and choose restful positions.

title: Diabetes: check blood sugar before intimacy
text: If you take insulin, intimacy is exercise — check your sugar and keep a snack nearby.

title: Intimacy after a pacemaker
text: People with pacemakers can usually return to normal sexual activity soon after recovery. Ask your cardiology team.

title: Angina and intimacy
text: If you get angina during exertion, ask your doctor whether to use your spray beforehand, and never combine it with erection tablets.

title: Erection tablets and blood pressure tablets
text: Some blood pressure tablets (alpha blockers) can lower blood pressure further with erection medicines. Ask about timing.

title: Erection creams and gels
text: Topical treatments for erections exist for men who can't take tablets. Ask your doctor.

title: Injections for erections
text: Penile injections are effective when tablets don't work. A specialist teaches safe use.

title: Penile implants are an option
text: For severe, lasting erection problems, implants have high satisfaction rates. A urologist can explain.

title: Shockwave therapy for erections
text: Low-intensity shockwave therapy is being studied for erection problems; evidence is still developing. Ask a urologist.

title: Testosterone isn't a cure for erections
text: Testosterone helps desire in men who are truly low, but most erection problems are about blood flow.

title: Women's libido and iron
text: Low iron causes tiredness that dampens desire. Women with heavy past periods or poor diet may be low.

title: Body confidence after mastectomy
text: Many women find a supportive bra, prosthesis or simply time and conversation help them feel confident again.

title: Intimacy after hysterectomy
text: Most women can resume intimacy about six weeks after a hysterectomy. Ask your surgeon.

title: Prostate cancer and orgasm
text: After prostate surgery, orgasm is usually still possible, even without ejaculation.

title: Couples therapy works later in life
text: Couples in their 60s and 70s benefit from counselling as much as younger couples.

title: Rebuild trust with small promises kept
text: Doing what you say you'll do, even small things, rebuilds trust in a relationship.

title: Apologise sincerely
text: A genuine 'I'm sorry' without 'but' repairs hurt faster than anything.

title: Hold your partner's hand during difficult talks
text: Physical touch during tough conversations lowers stress and keeps you on the same side.

title: Make a list of shared dreams
text: Talking about places you'd like to visit or things to try together brings excitement back.

title: Bring music into the bedroom
text: Music you both love sets a relaxed, romantic mood.

title: Soft lighting helps
text: Candles or a dim lamp feel romantic and flatter everyone.

title: Clean sheets, fresh start
text: Fresh bedding and a tidy room make the bedroom inviting.

title: Talk about contraception during perimenopause
text: Women can still conceive until periods have stopped for a year. Use contraception until then.

title: Single and curious? Learn about your body
text: Self-exploration helps you understand what feels good now, which helps with a future partner.

title: Dating apps for older adults
text: Many dating sites are designed for over-50s. Meet in public places and tell a friend where you are going.

title: Romance scams target older daters
text: Never send money to someone you've only met online, however convincing their story.

title: New partner? Talk about health early
text: Sharing health conditions and test results is caring, not awkward.

title: Gay and lesbian older adults deserve good care
text: Sexual health services welcome everyone. You shouldn't feel you have to hide who you are.

title: Mismatched desire after retirement
text: More time together can change a couple's rhythm. Talk about how much togetherness and space you each need.

title: Separate bedrooms don't mean less love
text: Some couples sleep better apart and plan intimate time together. That's fine.

title: Cuddle after waking
text: A few minutes of cuddling before getting up starts the day with warmth.

title: Desire and gratitude
text: People who feel appreciated by their partner report more desire.

title: Pay attention to your partner's stress
text: Helping your partner unwind — a cup of tea, a foot rub — often leads to closeness.

title: Accept the 'off' days
text: Not every attempt at intimacy goes to plan. Laughing it off keeps things relaxed.

title: Sex toys are common and normal
text: Many older adults use vibrators or other aids. They can help with reduced sensation and arthritis.

title: Choose body-safe materials
text: Medical-grade silicone toys are easier to clean and safer for sensitive skin.

title: Clean intimate products after use
text: Wash toys with warm water and mild soap and let them dry to prevent infections.

title: Desire after loss of a partner
text: Grief can switch desire off for a long time. That's normal; it may return when you're ready.

title: Talking to grown children about new relationships
text: Adult children may need time to adjust. Be honest and patient.

title: Intimacy in care homes
text: People in care settings still have the right to privacy and intimacy. Talk to staff about your needs.

title: Hormone patches and libido
text: For some women, hormone therapy improves libido by easing dryness, sleep and mood.

title: Vaginal estrogen with breast cancer history
text: Some women with past breast cancer can use low-dose vaginal estrogen; it's a decision for your cancer team.

title: Pelvic radiotherapy and intimacy
text: Radiotherapy can cause dryness and narrowing. Dilators and moisturisers help — ask your team early.

title: Erections after radiotherapy
text: Erection problems can appear months after prostate radiotherapy. Treatment can help.

title: Testicular shrinkage and hormones
text: Some hormone treatments for prostate cancer reduce desire and size. Support groups help men cope.

title: Desire and multiple sclerosis
text: MS can affect sensation and desire. Specialist nurses can offer practical help.

title: Parkinson's and intimacy
text: Parkinson's and its medicines can change desire, sometimes increasing it. Tell your specialist about changes.

title: Track hot flushes for a week before your appointment
text: Noting how many you have and how bad they are helps you and your doctor judge treatment.

title: Menopause and sleep: try a fan by the bed
text: Moving air feels cooler and helps you drift back to sleep after a night sweat.

title: Layer bedding, not just clothes
text: Two light blankets let you adjust quickly instead of one heavy duvet.

title: Cooling mattress toppers
text: Some women find gel or breathable toppers help with night sweats.

title: Menopause and alcohol-free drinks
text: Alcohol-free beers and wines let you join in socially without triggering flushes.

title: Menopause at work: keep a water bottle
text: Sipping cool water through the day helps with flushes and concentration.

title: Hot flushes and blood pressure
text: Women with frequent flushes should have their blood pressure checked regularly.

title: Menopause and calcium-rich snacks
text: Yoghurt, cheese, almonds and fortified plant milks are easy calcium boosters.

title: Menopause and vitamin K2
text: Fermented foods and cheese provide vitamin K2, which plays a role in bone health.

title: Gentle jumping helps bones
text: If your bones are healthy, small hops or skipping a few times a day can stimulate bone growth. Ask first if you have osteoporosis.

title: Osteoporosis: exercises to avoid
text: With osteoporosis, avoid deep forward bending and twisting under load. A physiotherapist can show safe exercises.

title: Menopause and posture
text: Upper-back exercises help prevent a rounded upper back that can develop with bone loss.

title: Menopause and protein needs
text: Women after menopause benefit from around 1–1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight daily, spread across meals.

title: Menopause and caffeine sensitivity
text: Many women find caffeine affects them more after menopause. Notice how you feel.

title: Menopause and anxiety at night
text: Waking with a racing heart is common. Slow breathing and a cool room help.

title: Menopause and short-term memory tricks
text: Writing things down and keeping routines helps through the foggy phase.

title: Menopause and dry eyes at the computer
text: Blink often, take breaks and use lubricating drops.

title: Menopause and nail changes
text: Brittle nails are common. Moisturise hands and nails and wear gloves for chores.

title: Menopause and body odour
text: Hot flushes can increase sweating. Breathable fabrics and regular showers help.

title: Menopause and tinnitus
text: Some women notice ringing in the ears around menopause. Mention it if it bothers you.

title: Menopause and burning mouth
text: A burning sensation in the mouth is more common after menopause. A dentist or doctor can help.

title: Menopause and electric-shock sensations
text: A brief electric feeling before a hot flush is a known symptom and harmless.

title: Menopause and itchy skin
text: Falling estrogen dries the skin. Emollients and lukewarm showers help.

title: Menopause and libido: you can ask for referral
text: Some areas have specialist menopause clinics for complex symptoms.

title: Menopause and depression history
text: Women with past depression are more likely to have mood symptoms at menopause — seek support early.

title: Menopause and premenstrual syndrome
text: PMS often worsens in perimenopause before improving after periods stop.

title: Menopause and migraine with aura
text: Women who have migraine with aura need specific advice about hormone therapy. Tell your doctor.

title: Menopause and blood clots history
text: If you've had a blood clot, transdermal estrogen may still be possible. Discuss carefully with your doctor.

title: Menopause and endometriosis
text: Women with past endometriosis need tailored hormone therapy advice.

title: Menopause and fibroids
text: Fibroids usually shrink after menopause, but hormone therapy may affect them. Ask your doctor.

title: Menopause and alcohol and bones
text: More than a couple of drinks a day speeds bone loss.

title: Menopause and smoking and bones
text: Smoking lowers estrogen further and weakens bones.

title: Menopause and walking with friends
text: Walking groups combine exercise, sunlight and company — three menopause helpers.

title: Menopause and gardening
text: Gardening is weight-bearing, calming and gets you outside.

title: Menopause and dancing
text: Dance classes are great weight-bearing exercise and lift mood.

title: Menopause and stretching for joint aches
text: A daily 10-minute stretch routine reduces stiffness.

title: Menopause and sleep hygiene
text: A regular bedtime, cool room and no screens before bed help menopausal sleep.

title: Menopause and night snacking
text: Hormone changes can increase cravings. Keep healthy options available in the evening.

title: Menopause and sugar
text: Cutting back on sugar may reduce energy dips and hot flushes for some women.

title: Menopause and fibre
text: Fibre helps with weight, cholesterol and digestion — all of which change at menopause.

title: Menopause and kindness to yourself
text: It's a big transition. Rest, ask for help, and give yourself credit.

title: Menopause: you're not alone
text: Around one billion women worldwide are in or past menopause. Sharing experiences helps.

title: Menopause and partners: share the facts
text: Partners who understand symptoms are more patient and supportive.

title: Menopause and humour
text: Many women find laughing about hot flushes with friends takes the sting out.

title: Menopause and new hobbies
text: Many women discover new passions after menopause — a time to put yourself first.

title: Menopause and checking moles
text: Hormone changes can coincide with skin changes. Check moles and see a doctor about changes.

title: Menopause and breast awareness
text: Know how your breasts normally look and feel and report any changes promptly.

title: Menopause and cervical screening
text: Keep going to cervical screening until your country's upper age limit.

title: Menopause and pelvic health check
text: If you notice heaviness, leaks or pain, ask for a pelvic health assessment.

title: Menopause and hair growth on the face
text: Some women notice more facial hair. It's common and can be managed with hair removal or treatments.

title: Menopause and acne
text: Hormone shifts can cause adult acne. A gentle routine and a pharmacist's advice help.

title: Menopause and voice changes
text: Some women notice a deeper or hoarser voice. Stay hydrated and mention it if persistent.

title: Menopause and gum bleeding
text: Hormone changes can make gums bleed more easily. Brush gently and see your dentist.

title: Menopause and restless legs
text: Restless legs can worsen around menopause. Check iron levels and stretch before bed.

title: Menopause and heart palpitations at night
text: If palpitations wake you with chest pain or breathlessness, seek urgent help.

title: Menopause and libido: physical closeness helps
text: Hugging and touch can keep desire alive even when hormones dip.

title: Menopause and changing friendships
text: This life stage often brings new friendships with other women going through the same.

title: Menopause and purpose
text: Many women find renewed energy for work, causes and creativity after menopause.

title: Menopause: treatment is a personal choice
text: There's no single right answer. Your symptoms, history and preferences guide the decision.

title: Men: know your blood pressure number
text: Men are more likely to have untreated high blood pressure. A quick check at a pharmacy is easy.

title: Prostate: limit spicy food if it irritates
text: Some men find spicy food and alcohol worsen urinary symptoms.

title: Bladder training for men
text: Gradually delaying urination helps men with urgency regain control.

title: Post-micturition dribble trick
text: Gently pressing behind the scrotum after urinating helps empty the urethra.

title: Sit to urinate at night
text: Sitting can help men empty the bladder more fully and avoids falls at night.

title: Men and incontinence after surgery
text: Pelvic floor exercises before and after prostate surgery speed recovery of bladder control.

title: Men and sunscreen on the scalp
text: Thinning hair exposes the scalp. Wear a hat or sunscreen.

title: Men's skin: moisturise too
text: Men's skin also dries with age. A simple moisturiser prevents itching.

title: Men and foot care
text: Thick nails and calluses are common. A podiatrist can help keep feet healthy.

title: Men and loneliness after bereavement
text: Widowed men are especially at risk of isolation. Reach out to friends and groups.

title: Men and cooking skills
text: Learning to cook simple healthy meals helps men living alone eat well.

title: Men and emotional health
text: Talking about feelings with a friend or counsellor is a strength, not a weakness.

title: Men and heart attack symptoms
text: Don't 'wait and see' with chest pain. Call emergency services.

title: Men and testosterone myths
text: Testosterone falls only slowly with age; big drops usually have a cause worth investigating.

title: Men and weightlifting safety
text: Use good form, start light and avoid holding your breath when lifting.

title: Men and back pain
text: Strong core muscles protect your back. Planks and bridges help.

title: Men and gout triggers
text: Beer, red meat and shellfish can trigger gout. Water and cherries may help.

title: Men and kidney stones
text: Drinking plenty of water and limiting salt reduce kidney stone risk.

title: Men and colon cancer screening
text: Men have a higher risk of bowel cancer. Do the screening test when invited.

title: Men and hearing protection
text: Wear ear protection when using mowers, drills and other loud tools.

title: Men and eye checks
text: Glaucoma is often symptomless. Regular eye tests protect your sight.

title: Men and depression after retirement
text: Losing a work identity can cause low mood. New routines and goals help.

title: Men and grandparenting
text: Time with grandchildren keeps men active, engaged and happy.

title: Men and volunteering
text: Volunteering gives purpose, structure and friendship after retirement.

title: Men and sleep
text: Men who snore loudly or stop breathing at night should be checked for sleep apnea.

title: Men and diabetes
text: Men often develop diabetes at a lower weight than women. Get your blood sugar checked.

title: Men and alcohol
text: Men are more likely to drink above safe limits. Have several alcohol-free days a week.

title: Men and smoking
text: Quitting at any age improves erections, breathing and heart health.

title: Men and anger
text: Uncontrolled anger raises blood pressure. Walking away and breathing slowly helps.

title: Men and bone fractures
text: Hip fractures in men are less common but more dangerous. Keep strong and prevent falls.

title: Morning stretch, all-day energy
text: Five minutes of stretching after waking loosens stiff muscles and gets blood flowing.

title: Sit by a window
text: Natural light through a window boosts alertness while you read or work.

title: Plan a daily 'energy walk'
text: A regular walk at the same time each day becomes a habit that lifts energy.

title: Eat a protein-rich lunch
text: Protein keeps blood sugar steady and prevents the afternoon slump.

title: Don't skip meals
text: Skipping meals leads to energy dips and overeating later.

title: Fruit and nuts for a steady snack
text: A piece of fruit with a few nuts gives quick and lasting energy.

title: Bananas before activity
text: A banana gives easy-to-digest energy before a walk or swim.

title: Oats for slow-release energy
text: Porridge releases energy slowly through the morning.

title: Energy and dehydration in winter
text: Heated rooms dry you out. Keep drinking in cold months too.

title: Swap the second coffee for water
text: Often tiredness in the afternoon is thirst, not a lack of caffeine.

title: Energy and noise
text: Constant noise is tiring. Seek quiet breaks in your day.

title: Short bursts of activity
text: Three 10-minute walks give the same benefit as one 30-minute walk.

title: Energy-boosting hobbies
text: Active hobbies like gardening, dancing and bowling give energy back.

title: Limit long sitting
text: Get up every half hour; even standing helps energy and circulation.

title: Fatigue after meals
text: Large, starchy meals cause drowsiness. Smaller, balanced meals keep you alert.

title: Energy and chronic illness
text: Pacing — spreading activity through the day with rests — helps conditions that cause fatigue.

title: Tired despite sleep? Check your mood
text: Low mood often feels like physical tiredness. Talk to someone.

title: Energy and medicines review
text: Beta blockers, antihistamines and some antidepressants can cause tiredness. Ask about alternatives.

title: Vitamin D and winter tiredness
text: Low vitamin D in winter can contribute to fatigue. A supplement is often advised.

title: Magnesium-rich foods for energy
text: Nuts, seeds and whole grains provide magnesium, needed for energy production.

title: Cold showers for alertness
text: A short cool rinse at the end of a shower wakes you up — skip it if you have heart problems.

title: Energy and good posture
text: Slouching restricts breathing and saps energy. Sit tall.

title: Get organised to save energy
text: Keep things you use often within easy reach to save effort.

title: Energy and positive company
text: Time with cheerful, supportive people is energising.

title: Rest before you're exhausted
text: Taking short rests before you're worn out helps you do more overall.

title: Afternoon tea break
text: A short break with a drink and a stretch refreshes energy.

title: Energy and breathing
text: Slow, deep belly breaths bring more oxygen and calm.

title: Sunlight on your face in the morning
text: A few minutes of morning sun signals your body to wake up.

title: Energy and listening to music
text: Upbeat music before a walk makes it feel easier.

title: Fatigue with fever or weight loss
text: Fatigue with fevers, night sweats or weight loss needs a doctor's check.

title: Breathlessness and fatigue
text: Getting breathless and tired doing less than usual should be checked.

title: Energy after surgery
text: Recovery takes energy. Expect to feel tired for weeks and build up slowly.

title: Energy and stress
text: Long-term stress is exhausting. Relaxation and support help.

title: Energy and gratitude
text: Focusing on what's going well lifts energy and mood.

title: Sleep better by getting up at the same time
text: A fixed wake-up time is the anchor of good sleep.

title: Bed for sleep only
text: Doing other activities in bed weakens the link between bed and sleep.

title: Get out of bed if you can't sleep
text: Lying awake for long periods trains your brain to be awake in bed.

title: Limit time in bed
text: Spending too long in bed can make sleep lighter. Match time in bed to the sleep you actually get.

title: Avoid heavy exercise late
text: Vigorous exercise within two hours of bed can make it harder to fall asleep.

title: A warm drink without caffeine
text: Herbal tea or warm milk can be part of a soothing routine.

title: Light snack if hungry
text: Going to bed hungry can wake you. A small snack is fine.

title: Sleep and room humidity
text: Very dry air can cause snoring and a dry throat. A humidifier may help.

title: Sleep and allergies
text: Dust mites in bedding can disturb sleep. Wash bedding hot weekly.

title: Sleep and blackout blinds in summer
text: Early sunrise can wake you. Blackout blinds help.

title: Sleep and street lights
text: Thick curtains or an eye mask block outside light.

title: Sleep and night-time worries
text: Keep a notepad by the bed to jot down worries.

title: Sleep and breathing exercises
text: Slow breathing switches on the body's calm response.

title: Sleep and late-night TV
text: Exciting or upsetting programmes before bed can keep you awake.

title: Sleep and tablets in bed
text: If you read on a tablet, use night mode and low brightness.

title: Sleep and clock-watching
text: Turn clocks away so you can't check the time.

title: Sleep and bathroom trips
text: Use a dim night light so you don't fully wake up.

title: Sleep and leg cramps
text: Stretching calves before bed may reduce night cramps. Mention frequent cramps to your doctor.

title: Sleep and heartburn
text: Avoid large meals, alcohol and spicy food in the evening.

title: Sleep and coughing at night
text: A persistent night cough can signal asthma, reflux or heart problems. Get it checked.

title: Sleep and pain
text: Good pain control at night helps sleep. Discuss timing with your doctor.

title: Sleep and itching
text: Moisturise before bed if dry skin keeps you awake.

title: Sleep and depression
text: Waking very early and not getting back to sleep can be a sign of depression.

title: Sleep and anxiety
text: Relaxation before bed and worry time earlier in the day help.

title: Sleep and grief
text: Grief disrupts sleep. Gentle routines and talking help.

title: Sleep and alcohol at dinner
text: Even a glass of wine with dinner can fragment sleep for some people.

title: Sleep and caffeine in chocolate
text: Chocolate contains some caffeine. Avoid large amounts in the evening.

title: Sleep and caffeine in tea
text: Black and green tea contain caffeine. Switch to herbal later in the day.

title: Sleep and nicotine
text: Nicotine patches can cause vivid dreams. Ask about removing them at night.

title: Sleep and medicine timing
text: Some medicines like diuretics are best taken in the morning to avoid night trips to the toilet.

title: Sleep and steroids
text: Steroid tablets can keep you awake. Take them in the morning if advised.

title: Sleep and daytime naps for carers
text: Carers often lose sleep. Short naps and respite care help.

title: Sleep and pets
text: Feed and settle pets before bed to avoid night waking.

title: Sleep and a comfortable pillow
text: Replace flat, lumpy pillows every couple of years.

title: Sleep and mattress age
text: Mattresses usually need replacing every 8–10 years.

title: Sleep and a cool feet trick
text: If you're too warm, put your feet outside the covers.

title: Sleep and warm hands
text: If you're cold, warm hands and feet help you fall asleep.

title: Sleep and a bedtime story
text: Listening to a calm audiobook can help the mind wind down.

title: Sleep and prayer or reflection
text: Ending the day with reflection or prayer brings calm.

title: Sleep and gratitude
text: Thinking of three good things as you lie down promotes calm.

title: Sleep and restless mind
text: Count backwards from 300 in threes to occupy a busy mind.

title: Sleep and journaling
text: Writing a few lines before bed can settle thoughts.

title: Sleep and morning light walks
text: Morning light walks help you feel sleepy earlier at night.

title: Sleep and holiday time changes
text: Adjust bedtime gradually before travel across time zones.

title: Sleep and jet lag
text: Get outside in daylight at your destination to reset your body clock.

title: Sleep and shift in older age
text: Many people naturally become earlier risers with age. Go with it if it suits you.

title: Sharper focus with a daily walk
text: Walking boosts blood flow to the brain and improves attention for hours.

text: Regularly challenging your mind helps maintain memory.

title: Learn a poem by heart
text: Memorising a short poem exercises memory and brings pleasure.

title: Sing songs you know
text: Singing familiar songs exercises memory and lifts mood.

title: Try a new recipe
text: Following a new recipe exercises planning and memory.

title: Learn the names of birds
text: Bird-watching and learning their songs is great memory training outdoors.

title: Plant names in the garden
text: Learning plant names challenges memory while you garden.

title: Play word games
text: Word games like Scrabble build vocabulary and memory.

text: Healthy blood pressure is one of the best things for your brain.

title: Brain and blood sugar
text: Stable blood sugar protects small blood vessels in the brain.

title: Brain and alcohol
text: Keeping within low-risk limits protects memory.

title: Brain and loneliness
text: Social contact protects the brain. Call a friend today.

title: Brain and hearing
text: Hearing aids help the brain stay engaged with conversation.

title: Brain and eyesight
text: Clear vision keeps you reading and socialising.

title: Brain and sleep
text: Good sleep clears brain waste and consolidates memories.

title: Brain and stress
text: Calming practices protect memory from stress hormones.

title: Brain and physical fitness
text: Fitter people tend to have better memory in later life.

title: Brain and dancing
text: Learning dance steps is excellent brain exercise.

title: Brain and second languages
text: Learning even a few words of a new language challenges the brain.

title: Brain and art
text: Painting and drawing engage planning and visual memory.

title: Brain and storytelling
text: Telling stories to grandchildren exercises memory and language.

title: Brain and history
text: Reading about history gives the brain new information to organise.

title: Brain and travel
text: Exploring new places stimulates memory and curiosity.

title: Brain and a positive attitude
text: People who believe ageing is positive tend to have better memory.

title: Brain and routines
text: Routines free mental energy for new learning.

title: Brain and a daily diary
text: A diary helps memory and gives a record of your life.

title: Brain and mindful attention
text: Paying full attention when you put things down helps you find them later.

title: Brain and visual images
text: Linking information to vivid pictures improves recall.

title: Brain and chunking
text: Group information into small chunks to remember it.

title: Brain and teaching
text: Teaching others strengthens your own understanding.

title: Brain and mental maths
text: Adding up shopping in your head keeps number skills sharp.

title: Brain and olive oil
text: Olive oil is a key part of brain-friendly Mediterranean eating.

title: Brain and berries
text: Regular berries are linked with slower memory decline.

title: Brain and coffee
text: Moderate coffee is not harmful to the brain and may help alertness.

title: Brain and head injury prevention
text: Wear a helmet when cycling and prevent falls.

title: Brain and confusion after surgery
text: Older adults can be confused after surgery. It usually passes; tell the team if it doesn't.

title: Brain and delirium
text: Sudden confusion needs urgent medical attention.

title: Brain and memory testing
text: A memory assessment can give reassurance or early help.

title: Brain and family history
text: A family history of dementia doesn't mean you'll get it. Healthy habits still help.

title: Brain and puzzles with others
text: Puzzle clubs combine thinking and friendship.

title: Brain and volunteering
text: Volunteering keeps the mind active and connected.

title: Brain and meditation
text: Meditation may improve attention and reduce stress.

title: Brain and gratitude
text: Positive emotions support thinking and memory.

title: Healthier heart with less sitting
text: Breaking up sitting time every 30 minutes helps blood sugar and blood pressure.

title: Eat fibre for your heart
text: Fibre from oats, beans and vegetables lowers cholesterol.

title: Choose lean protein
text: Fish, poultry and beans are heart-friendly protein choices.

title: Unsalted nuts as snacks
text: Nuts provide healthy fats that support the heart.

title: Swap white for wholegrain
text: Whole grains protect the heart better than refined grains.

title: Use olive or rapeseed oil
text: These oils contain heart-healthy unsaturated fats.

title: Cut down on cheese
text: Cheese is salty and high in saturated fat — enjoy in smaller portions.

title: Choose low-salt stock
text: Stock cubes are very salty. Choose low-salt versions or make your own.

title: Rinse tinned beans
text: Rinsing tinned beans and vegetables removes some salt.

title: Check bread labels
text: Bread is a major source of salt. Compare brands.

title: Heart and potassium
text: Potatoes, bananas and beans provide potassium to help balance salt.

title: Heart and flavonoids
text: Tea, berries and apples contain flavonoids linked with heart health.

title: Heart and fish oil
text: Eating fish is better than supplements for most people.

title: Heart and beetroot
text: Beetroot juice may lower blood pressure a little.

title: Heart and dark leafy greens
text: Greens provide nitrates and folate for healthy blood vessels.

title: Heart and portion control
text: Smaller portions help manage weight and heart health.

title: Heart and sugar
text: High sugar diets raise heart risk. Cut back on sweet drinks and snacks.

title: Heart and alcohol
text: Drinking within limits helps blood pressure and heart rhythm.

title: Heart and cycling
text: Cycling is great cardio exercise, on the road or a stationary bike.

title: Heart and swimming
text: Swimming strengthens the heart without stressing joints.

title: Heart and stretching
text: Stretching helps you stay active for heart exercise.

title: Heart and gratitude
text: Positive emotions are linked with better heart health.

title: Heart and music
text: Calm music can lower heart rate and blood pressure.

title: Heart and home blood pressure monitors
text: A validated home monitor helps track your numbers.

text: Take two readings a minute apart and record the average.

title: Heart and white-coat effect
text: Blood pressure can be higher at the doctor's. Home readings give a fuller picture.

title: Heart and statins myths
text: Statins are well studied and safe for most people. Ask questions if you're worried.

title: Heart and cholesterol targets
text: Your doctor will set targets based on your overall risk.

title: Heart and family history
text: Tell your doctor if close relatives had heart disease young.

title: Heart and diabetes
text: Diabetes doubles heart risk. Good control helps.

title: Heart and kidney disease
text: Kidney disease raises heart risk. Keep blood pressure controlled.

title: Heart and flu
text: Flu can trigger heart attacks. Get vaccinated.

title: Heart and cold weather
text: Wrap up warmly in winter to protect your heart.

title: Heart and heat
text: Very hot weather strains the heart. Stay cool and drink water.

title: Heart and atrial fibrillation
text: An irregular pulse can mean atrial fibrillation. It's treatable.

title: Heart and anticoagulants
text: If prescribed blood thinners for AF, take them regularly to prevent strokes.

title: Heart and stroke prevention
text: Controlling blood pressure is the single biggest way to prevent strokes.

title: Heart and TIA warning
text: A brief stroke-like episode that resolves still needs urgent assessment.

title: Heart and heart failure diet
text: With heart failure, your team may advise on salt and fluid limits.

title: Heart and swollen legs
text: Leg swelling can have many causes; persistent swelling needs checking.

title: Heart and fainting
text: Fainting during exercise needs urgent medical attention.

title: Heart and chest pain at rest
text: Chest pain at rest lasting more than a few minutes — call emergency services.

title: Heart and cardiac rehab classes
text: Rehab classes are safe, supportive and speed recovery.

title: Heart and intimacy after events
text: Ask your rehab team when intimacy is safe again.

title: Heart and driving after a heart attack
text: Rules vary — ask your doctor when you can drive.

title: Heart and returning to activity
text: Build up gradually after heart events, following advice.

title: Heart and knowing CPR
text: Learning CPR could save a life — including your partner's.

title: Easier mornings with bedtime stretches
text: Gentle stretches before bed reduce morning stiffness in hips and back.

title: Knee pain: try straight-leg raises
text: Lying down and lifting a straight leg a few inches strengthens the thigh without bending the knee.

title: Hip pain: clamshell exercise
text: Lying on your side, knees bent, lift the top knee to strengthen hip muscles.

title: Back pain: cat-cow stretch
text: On hands and knees, gently arch and round your back to ease stiffness.

title: Neck pain: check your pillow height
text: Your pillow should keep your neck level with your spine.

title: Shoulder pain: wall walks
text: Walk your fingers up a wall to gently improve shoulder movement.

title: Hand arthritis: warm water exercises
text: Moving your fingers in warm water eases stiffness.

title: Wrist pain: rest from repetitive tasks
text: Take breaks from knitting, typing or gardening to rest your wrists.

title: Foot pain: roll a ball under your foot
text: Rolling a tennis ball under the sole eases foot pain.

title: Ankle stiffness: ankle alphabet
text: Draw the alphabet in the air with your toes to loosen ankles.

title: Joint pain and weather
text: Many people feel more pain in cold, damp weather. Stay warm and active.

title: Joint pain and stress
text: Stress makes pain feel worse. Relaxation helps.

title: Joint pain and posture
text: Good posture reduces strain on neck and back.

title: Joint pain and walking aids
text: A stick can take load off a painful hip or knee.

title: Joint pain and pacing
text: Spread tasks through the day to avoid flare-ups.

title: Joint pain and physiotherapy
text: A physio can design exercises for your joints.

title: Joint pain and occupational therapy
text: An OT can suggest gadgets to make tasks easier.

title: Joint pain and hydrotherapy
text: Warm pools ease pain and make exercise easier.

title: Joint pain and tai chi
text: Tai chi improves pain and function in knee arthritis.

title: Joint pain and cycling
text: Cycling builds leg strength with little joint impact.

title: Joint pain and gardening tools
text: Long-handled tools reduce bending and kneeling.

title: Joint pain and kitchen gadgets
text: Jar openers and lightweight pans protect hands.

title: Joint pain and getting up
text: Use your legs, not your back, to stand from low chairs.

title: Joint pain and car seats
text: A cushion can make getting in and out of cars easier.

title: Joint pain and reaching
text: Use a step stool safely or a reacher instead of overstretching.

title: Joint pain and carrying
text: Use a backpack or trolley rather than carrying heavy bags on one side.

title: Gout and cherries
text: Some studies suggest cherries may reduce gout attacks.

title: Gout and water
text: Drinking plenty of water helps the body clear uric acid.

title: Gout and medicines
text: If you have frequent gout, preventive medicine can stop attacks.

text: Movement helps cartilage stay healthy; it's not simply worn out by use.

title: Rheumatoid arthritis and exercise
text: Exercise is safe and helpful with rheumatoid arthritis when tailored.

text: Sudden shoulder and hip stiffness in older adults can be PMR, which responds to treatment.

title: Osteoporosis and fracture risk
text: Medicine plus exercise and fall prevention cuts fracture risk.

text: Sudden back pain after minor strain may be a spinal fracture from osteoporosis.

text: Pain down the leg from the back often improves with movement and time.

title: Spinal stenosis
text: Leg pain when walking that eases when bending forward may be spinal stenosis.

title: Hip pain and lying down
text: A pillow between knees eases hip pain at night.

title: Stronger legs with daily chair stands
text: Ten slow sit-to-stands a day build leg strength for life.

title: Balance training while waiting for the kettle
text: Stand on one leg holding the counter while the kettle boils.

title: Practise turning safely
text: Take small steps when turning to avoid losing balance.

title: Strength and confidence
text: Feeling strong makes you more confident to go out.

title: Use household items as weights
text: Water bottles and tins make easy hand weights.

title: Strength and resistance bands
text: Bands come in different strengths — start light.

text: Pulling a band toward you strengthens your upper back and posture.

text: Pressing light weights overhead strengthens shoulders for reaching.

text: Stepping up onto a low step strengthens legs.

title: Strength: wall sits
text: Leaning against a wall with knees slightly bent builds thigh strength.

title: Strength: calf raises
text: Rise onto toes to strengthen calves for walking.

text: A gentle side plank against a wall strengthens hips and core.

text: Practise bending from the hips with a straight back to protect your spine.

text: Standing with eyes closed while holding a counter challenges balance.

title: Balance: standing up from the floor
text: Practising getting up from the floor builds confidence.

text: Stand up slowly and tell your doctor about dizziness.

text: Little and often beats occasional big efforts.

text: Combine strength exercise with good protein when losing weight.

text: Upper tummy pain spreading to the back with weight loss should be checked.

text: Yearly diabetic eye screening prevents sight loss.

text: Leafy greens and colourful vegetables support eye health.

text: Olive oil drops can soften wax. See a nurse if blocked.

text: Ear problems can cause dizziness; see a doctor if it persists.

title: Ears and tinnitus relief
text: Background sounds and relaxation help tinnitus.

text: Spit out toothpaste without rinsing to keep fluoride on teeth.

text: Brushing before bed is the most important brush of the day.

text: Bleeding, receding or loose teeth need a dental check.

text: Clean dentures with a brush and denture cleaner, not toothpaste.

title: Teeth and heart

text: If your sense of smell is weak, use smoke and gas alarms.

text: Some medicines change taste; ask your pharmacist.

text: Test bath water with your elbow if you have reduced sensation.

text: A spot that doesn't heal in weeks needs checking.

text: Keep wounds clean and covered; see a nurse if they don't heal.

text: Leg ulcers need specialist care; don't ignore them.

title: Skin and pressure
text: Change position regularly to prevent pressure sores.

text: See a doctor quickly about a painful rash on one side.

text: Gradual thinning is normal; sudden loss needs checking.

text: See a podiatrist for thick nails, corns or diabetes.

text: Having a reason to get up each day protects wellbeing.

text: Leaks are common and treatable — don't let them keep you home.

text: New or worsening breathlessness needs assessment.

title: Leftover vegetables make the best soup

title: A tin of fish is a ready meal
text: Keep tinned salmon, sardines or mackerel in the cupboard for a quick, protein-rich meal on toast or with salad.

title: Two eggs make a meal in five minutes
text: Scrambled or poached eggs on wholegrain toast give protein, vitamin D and B12 when you're short on time or energy.

title: Beans on toast is a balanced meal
text: Baked beans on wholegrain toast provide protein, fibre and slow-release energy. Choose reduced-salt and -sugar beans.

title: Garlic and onion make healthy food taste great
text: Softly frying onion and garlic in olive oil is the base of countless healthy dishes and reduces the need for salt.

title: Dried herbs are as useful as fresh
text: A cupboard of dried oregano, thyme and basil adds flavour to stews and sauces in seconds, without salt.

title: Lemon makes vegetables sing
text: A squeeze of lemon on greens, fish or soup brightens flavour so you reach for the salt less.

title: Greek yoghurt for twice the protein
text: Strained Greek-style yoghurt has about twice the protein of regular yoghurt. Top with fruit for a filling snack.

title: Eat your fruit rather than drink it
text: A whole orange keeps its fibre and fills you up; a glass of juice delivers the sugar without the fibre.

title: Frozen berries all winter
text: Frozen berries are picked at their best and keep their nutrients. Stir them into porridge or yoghurt year-round.

title: Two kiwis a day for regularity
text: Studies show eating two kiwi fruit a day helps relieve constipation as well as some remedies.

title: Avocado for creamy, healthy fats
text: Avocado on toast or in salad gives healthy fats and fibre — a good swap for butter.

title: Sweet potato for a fibre-rich side
text: Baked sweet potato provides fibre and vitamin A and keeps you full.

title: Carrots support night vision
text: Carrots are rich in beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A for healthy eyes.

title: Spinach for folate and iron
text: A handful of spinach stirred into soups or eggs adds folate and some iron.

title: Frozen peas add protein to any meal
text: Peas are a surprising source of plant protein and fibre — keep a bag in the freezer.

title: Hummus makes vegetables a snack
text: Dipping carrot or pepper sticks in hummus is a satisfying snack with protein and fibre.

title: A handful of almonds for bones
text: Almonds provide calcium, magnesium and vitamin E — good for bones and skin.

title: Walnuts for your heart and brain
text: Walnuts contain plant omega-3 fats linked with heart and brain health. A small handful a day is enough.

title: Pumpkin seeds for zinc
text: A sprinkle of pumpkin seeds adds zinc, which supports immunity, healing and taste.

title: Salmon once a week for omega-3 and vitamin D
text: Fresh, frozen or tinned salmon provides omega-3 for heart and brain, and vitamin D for bones.

title: Mackerel: the budget superfood
text: Mackerel is one of the richest, cheapest sources of omega-3. Smoked mackerel on toast makes a quick meal.

title: Remove chicken skin to cut fat
text: Most of the fat in chicken is in the skin. Removing it makes a leaner meal.

title: Choose lean mince for healthier sauces
text: Lower-fat mince, browned and drained, makes healthier bolognese and chilli.

title: Swap white rice for brown
text: Brown rice has more fibre and nutrients and raises blood sugar more slowly.

title: Wholewheat pasta keeps you fuller
text: Wholewheat pasta has around three times the fibre of white pasta.

title: Quinoa is a complete protein
text: Quinoa provides all the essential amino acids — a good base for salads and bowls.

title: Barley in soup lowers cholesterol
text: Barley contains beta-glucan fibre, which helps lower cholesterol.

title: Rye bread keeps hunger at bay
text: Dense rye bread is high in fibre and keeps you satisfied longer than white bread.

title: A square of dark chocolate satisfies
text: Dark chocolate with 70% or more cocoa satisfies a sweet tooth with less sugar.

title: Warm milk before bed
text: A warm milky drink provides protein and calcium and makes a relaxing bedtime ritual.

title: Soup counts toward your fluids
text: A bowl of soup provides fluid as well as nutrients — handy if you find drinking water hard.

title: Eating out? Choose grilled over fried
text: Grilled fish or chicken with vegetables is lighter and healthier than fried options.

title: Ask for extra vegetables when eating out
text: Most restaurants will swap chips for vegetables or salad if you ask.

title: Share a starter or dessert
text: Sharing dishes lets you enjoy a treat with half the calories.

title: Start your shop in the fruit and veg aisle
text: Filling your basket with fresh produce first leaves less room for processed food.

title: Compare salt on labels
text: Similar foods can vary widely in salt. Comparing two brands can halve your intake.

title: Seasonal produce tastes better and costs less
text: Fruit and vegetables in season are cheaper, fresher and more flavourful.

title: Cook once, eat twice
text: Make double portions and freeze half for an easy healthy meal on a tired day.

title: One-pot meals save effort
text: Stews and casseroles cooked in one pot are nutritious and leave little washing up.

title: Roast vegetables for natural sweetness
text: Roasting carrots, peppers and squash with a little olive oil brings out their sweetness.

title: Steam vegetables to keep vitamins
text: Steaming keeps more vitamins than boiling and leaves vegetables bright and crunchy.

title: Freeze soup in single portions
text: Freezing soup in single servings means a healthy lunch is always minutes away.

title: Put your fork down between bites
text: Slowing down lets your body notice fullness and helps digestion.

title: A yearly check-up catches problems early
text: Many serious conditions — high blood pressure, diabetes, some cancers — have no early symptoms. A yearly check finds them while they're easier to treat.

title: Order repeat prescriptions a week ahead
text: Running out of regular medicines can be risky. Ordering early avoids gaps over weekends and holidays.

title: Your pharmacist can save you a doctor's visit
text: Pharmacists can advise on coughs, colds, rashes and minor aches, and tell you when you do need a doctor.

title: Keep your fridge at 5°C or below
text: A fridge thermometer helps keep food at a safe temperature and prevents food poisoning.

title: Eat leftovers within two days
text: Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate them, and eat within two days to stay safe.

title: Heatwave plan: close curtains early
text: Keeping curtains closed on sunny sides in the morning keeps rooms much cooler later in the day.

title: Cold snap plan: heat your main room
text: Keep the room you spend most time in at least 18°C, and wear layers rather than one thick jumper.

title: Smoke alarms on every floor
text: A working smoke alarm on each level of your home gives you time to escape a fire.

title: Hang up on 'miracle cure' calls
text: Genuine treatments aren't sold by cold calls. Check anything health-related with your doctor or pharmacist.

title: Know where your nearest defibrillator is
text: Public defibrillators are in many shops and stations. Knowing where yours is could save a life.

title: Learn hands-only CPR
text: Pushing hard and fast in the centre of the chest keeps blood flowing until help arrives. A short course builds confidence.

title: Keep a symptoms diary before appointments
text: Writing down when symptoms happen and what makes them better or worse helps your doctor find the cause.

title: Ask for a second opinion when it matters
text: For big decisions like surgery, it is reasonable to ask for another specialist's view.

title: Keep emergency numbers where you can see them
text: A list of emergency numbers and family contacts by the phone saves precious time.

title: A medical alert pendant brings help fast
text: If you live alone or have fallen before, a pendant alarm can call for help at the press of a button.

title: Warm baths ease stiff muscles
text: A 15-minute warm bath relaxes tight muscles and eases aches before bed.

title: Heat wraps for back pain
text: Low-level heat wraps worn for a few hours can ease lower back pain.

title: Cold packs for fresh swelling
text: For a new sprain or swelling, a cold pack wrapped in a towel for 15 minutes helps.

title: Support sore joints with pillows
text: Pillows under the knees or between the legs ease pain in bed.

title: Swimming takes weight off painful joints
text: Water supports your weight, so you can move painful joints more freely.

title: Tai chi eases chronic pain
text: Studies show tai chi can reduce pain and stiffness in arthritis and back pain.

title: Slow breathing turns down pain
text: Slow, deep breathing calms the nervous system and can lessen how strong pain feels.

title: Keep your mind busy to ease pain
text: Absorbing activities — a film, a phone call, a puzzle — reduce how much attention pain gets.

title: Better sleep means less pain
text: Pain feels worse after a bad night. Improving sleep often eases chronic pain.

title: Pain support groups help
text: Talking with others who live with pain gives practical tips and less isolation.

title: Count all your paracetamol
text: Cold and flu remedies often contain paracetamol too. Check labels so you don't take too much.

title: Opioid painkillers need careful use
text: Strong painkillers can cause constipation, drowsiness and falls. Use them only as prescribed and review regularly.

title: Nerve pain needs different medicines
text: Burning or shooting nerve pain often responds to different medicines from ordinary painkillers. Ask your doctor.

title: Try a TENS machine for some pain
text: A TENS machine sends gentle electrical pulses through the skin and helps some people with back and joint pain.

title: Acupuncture helps some people
text: Some people with back pain or headaches find acupuncture helpful. Use a qualified practitioner.

title: Headaches? Drink a glass of water first
text: Mild dehydration is a common cause of headaches. Try water before reaching for a tablet.

title: Screen breaks prevent headaches
text: Look away from screens every 20 minutes to reduce eye strain and headaches.

title: Cutting caffeine suddenly can cause headaches
text: Reduce coffee gradually to avoid withdrawal headaches.

title: New headaches after 50 need checking
text: A new type of headache in later life, especially with scalp tenderness or jaw pain, should be checked promptly.

title: Sit with your back supported
text: A cushion in the small of your back helps keep a healthy curve and prevents back ache.

title: Strong core muscles protect your back
text: Gentle core exercises like bridges and pelvic tilts help prevent back pain.

title: A supportive mattress for a happier back
text: If you wake stiff and sore, your mattress may be too soft or worn out.

title: Walk a little further each week to breathe easier
text: Gradually increasing your walking strengthens your breathing muscles and reduces breathlessness.

title: Singing strengthens breathing
text: Singing teaches you to control your breath and is used in programmes for lung disease.

title: Belly breathing for breathlessness
text: Breathing deeply into your belly, with a hand on it to feel it rise, uses your lungs more efficiently.

title: A smoke-free home protects everyone's lungs
text: Smoking outside, away from doors and windows, protects family and pets.

title: Ventilate when using wood stoves
text: Wood smoke irritates the lungs. Make sure stoves are well maintained and rooms ventilated.

title: Fragrance-free cleaning products are kinder to lungs
text: Strong sprays and bleach can irritate airways. Open windows when cleaning.

title: Treat damp and mould promptly
text: Mould spores worsen asthma and chest problems. Ventilate and clean mould as soon as it appears.

title: Damp-dust to keep dust down
text: A damp cloth traps dust instead of spreading it into the air.

title: High pollen? Keep windows closed
text: On high-pollen days, keep windows closed and shower after being outdoors.

title: Exercise away from busy roads
text: Walking in parks or quiet streets reduces the traffic fumes you breathe in.

title: Have your inhaler technique checked
text: Up to half of people use inhalers incorrectly. A pharmacist can check yours in minutes.

title: Carry your reliever inhaler
text: If you have asthma or COPD, keep your reliever inhaler with you at all times.

title: A yearly asthma review
text: An annual review makes sure your treatment still fits your needs.

title: Know your COPD action plan
text: An action plan tells you what to do when breathing gets worse, so you can act early.

title: Lungs recover after quitting
text: Within months of stopping smoking, coughing and breathlessness often improve.

title: Chest infections: get help early
text: In older adults, chest infections can worsen quickly. See a doctor if you're getting worse.

title: Coughing up blood is urgent
text: Coughing up blood should always be checked by a doctor quickly.

title: A cough that lasts three weeks
text: A cough lasting more than three weeks should be checked, especially if you smoke or have smoked.

title: Swap soap for an emollient wash
text: Soap-free washes clean without drying older skin.

title: Reapply sunscreen every two hours
text: Sunscreen wears off with time, sweat and towels. Reapply when outdoors.

title: Seek shade at midday
text: The sun is strongest between 11 am and 3 pm in summer. Plan outdoor time around it.

title: A wide-brimmed hat protects ears and neck
text: Ears and the back of the neck are common places for skin cancer. A wide brim covers them.

title: Calm itchy skin with cotton and coolness
text: Cotton clothing, cool rooms and moisturiser help itchy skin; scratching makes it worse.

title: Protein helps skin heal
text: Protein, vitamin C and zinc from food help wounds and skin heal.

title: Stop smoking for brighter skin
text: Smoking reduces blood flow to the skin. Quitting improves colour and healing.

title: Stress can flare up skin conditions
text: Eczema and psoriasis often flare with stress. Relaxation can help.

title: Be gentle with thinning hair
text: Avoid tight hairstyles, harsh dyes and very hot styling tools.

title: Moisturise your nails
text: Rub hand cream into nails and cuticles to prevent splitting.

title: Wear gloves for chores
text: Rubber gloves for washing up and garden gloves protect hands and nails.

title: Moisturise feet — but not between the toes
text: Dry heels crack easily. Moisturise them, but keep between the toes dry to avoid infection.

title: Fresh socks every day
text: Clean, breathable socks help prevent fungal infections and odour.

title: Cut toenails straight across
text: Cutting straight across helps prevent painful ingrown toenails.

title: Walk on grass and gravel to train balance
text: Uneven ground makes your ankles and balance work harder — hold a stick if needed.

title: Look ahead, not down, when walking
text: Looking ahead improves posture and balance and helps you spot hazards earlier.

title: Seated leg lifts strengthen thighs
text: Sitting tall, straighten one knee and hold for five seconds. Repeat 10 times each leg.

title: Squeeze a ball for a stronger grip
text: Squeezing a soft ball for a few seconds, 10 times a day, builds grip for jars and bags.

title: Shift your weight to train balance
text: Holding the counter, slowly shift your weight from one foot to the other.

title: Sideways steps along the counter
text: Stepping sideways strengthens hip muscles that keep you steady.

title: Remove trip hazards today
text: Loose rugs, trailing cables and clutter cause many falls. Clear walkways now.

title: Grab rails in the bathroom prevent falls
text: Fitting rails by the toilet and bath is one of the most effective fall-prevention steps.

title: Muscles need rest days
text: Leave a day between strength sessions for the same muscles so they can rebuild.

title: Track your repetitions to see progress
text: Writing down how many chair stands or lifts you do shows how much stronger you're getting.

title: Make text bigger on your phone
text: Increasing text size in settings reduces eye strain.

title: Use glaucoma drops every day
text: Glaucoma drops prevent sight loss only when used every day, even if your eyes feel fine.

title: Spare reading glasses in every room
text: Keeping a pair where you read saves strain and searching.

title: Keep hearing aid batteries in your bag
text: Spare batteries or a charging case mean you're never left without sound.

title: Turn on subtitles
text: Subtitles on the TV help you follow programmes and reduce listening fatigue.

title: Fluoride toothpaste twice a day
text: Brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste protects teeth and roots.

title: Keep sweet things to mealtimes
text: Sugar between meals feeds the bacteria that cause decay.

title: Take dentures out at night
text: Leaving dentures out overnight lets gums rest and reduces infections.

title: Mouth sores over three weeks need checking
text: An ulcer or patch that doesn't heal should be seen by a dentist or doctor.

title: Check foods by date, not smell
text: If your sense of smell has faded, rely on use-by dates to stay safe.

title: Spread drinks through the day
text: Drinking evenly through the day is easier on the bladder than large amounts at once.

title: Decaf can calm an urgent bladder
text: Caffeine irritates the bladder. Switching to decaf often reduces urgency.

title: Fizzy drinks can trigger urgency
text: Carbonated drinks irritate the bladder for some people.

title: Losing weight reduces leaks
text: Extra weight presses on the bladder. Losing even a little can help.

title: Toilet at set times
text: Going at regular times can reduce accidents while you retrain your bladder.

title: A night light to the toilet
